title: Water Confidence: The Event Nobody Trains For Until It's Too Late
summary: CWSA doesn't measure swim skill — it measures whether you can stay functional in water when you're encumbered and mildly panicked. It's the most preventable failure at Mackall, and it takes months of pool time to fix.
takeaways: Water confidence is autonomic regulation under a specific stressor, not swim fitness — cardio doesn't transfer
CWSA has three graded tasks: 15m equipment swim, 3m blindfold drop, equipment ditch — pass all or re-test
Walton's four-stage progression: face-in-water, bobs, restricted-movement laps, task-under-load
Biggest predictor of failure is zero deliberate water exposure in the year before ship
Building the Elite guests agree: comfort in water = exposure hours, not talent
tfvoodoo — treat CWSA as psychological, not athletic; showing up having never swum in boots is preventable
7th Group runs riverine and jungle ops across SOUTHCOM — water is a working environment, not a checkbox
Two 30-minute pool sessions per week for 12 months and you show up with the assessment already won

skills.title: Bobs for CO2 tolerance
skills.detail: Sink to shallow-end bottom, exhale slowly, push off, inhale, sink again. Ten in a row. Teaches your nervous system that being underwater is not dying.

skills.title: Clothed swim progression
skills.detail: Start in a t-shirt, add sweatpants, then boots (or old running shoes if facility bans boots). Familiarizes the proprioceptive weirdness before it happens with a grader watching.

skills.title: Twice-weekly pool discipline
skills.detail: Thirty minutes, two sessions, non-negotiable. Community rec center, YMCA, base pool — anything 25m or longer. Calendar it now, not later.

homework: This week, locate a pool you have consistent access to, and put two 30-minute sessions on your calendar for next week.
source: Ruck Up or Shut Up (Walton, 2023) — water confidence chapter; supported by TC 3-22.9 / Combat Water Survival doctrine and Building the Elite drownproofing episodes

title: Peer Evals: The Filter Nobody Prepares For
summary: Peer evaluations end more SF careers than any single physical event, and almost nobody trains for them on purpose. Walton, tfvoodoo, and the humility default.
takeaways: Peer evals are on the board's table next to your PT card and land nav score — guys who pass every event get peered out every class.
Walton's two failure modes on team week: the guy who disappears, and the guy who won't shut up. Both get peered.
Structurally invisible during good moments, structurally present during bad ones — that's the top-scored peer.
Peer scores are relative, not absolute, and reputation locks in inside the first 48 hours of team week.
tfvoodoo's three archetypes that get peered every time: too-gray gray man, the talker, and the guy who thinks he's better than his peers.
Humility default — treat every peer as if they might make it and you might not.
Surplus physical capacity is what lets you help the guy next to you; if you're maxed on your own ruck, you can't peer well.
Rehearse being the second-loudest person in the room — that's a trainable habit, not a personality trait.

skills.title: Talk-to-listen audit
skills.detail: Pick one daily setting and count how often you talk vs. listen. Adjust the ratio. Runs continuously, no equipment needed.

skills.title: Take the heavy end first
skills.detail: In any group physical task, volunteer for the harder position while you're fresh, rotate off cleanly. Builds the peer signature Walton names.

skills.title: Second-loudest rehearsal
skills.detail: Contribute, execute, then shut up when someone else has the floor. Practice in low-stakes settings so it's automatic at Mackall.

homework: This week, pick one setting you're in daily and count how many times you talk versus how many times you listen. Adjust the ratio.
source: Ruck Up or Shut Up (Walton, 2023) — team-week chapter; tfvoodoo r/specialforces standup

title: Land Nav: The Skill That Decides the Star Course
summary: Land nav is the most trainable event at SFAS and the one candidates show up under-prepared for. Twelve months out, you build it in layers — fundamentals, terrain association, attack points, decision-making under fatigue.
takeaways: Land nav is a physical skill executed under cognitive load — plotting grids tired, cold, and wet is a different task than doing it at a picnic table.
TC 3-25.26 (chapters 3, 5, 9, 11) is the doctrinal source of truth — put a PDF on your phone this week.
Walton's four layers in Ruck Up or Shut Up: fundamentals cold, terrain association, attack points and catch features, decisions under fatigue.
Know five pace counts, not one — flat/up/down, day/night, loaded/unloaded, fresh/after 10 miles.
Terrain associators with dead reckoning as backup finish the Star Course. Not the other way around.
tfvoodoo's rule: buy a Cammenga tritium lensatic, use paper maps, and get lost on purpose.
Terrain avoidance is planning, not weakness — selection is a distance event, not a strength event.
Water confidence and swimming are non-negotiable and non-crammable — start now if you're not strong in a pool.

skills.title: Pace count in five conditions
skills.detail: Measure your 100m pace on flat ground, uphill, downhill, at night, and after a 10-mile ruck. Log all five and re-verify quarterly.

skills.title: Attack points and catch features
skills.detail: Never nav directly to an objective. Nav to a definite terrain feature nearby, then shoot a short precise azimuth to the box. Identify a catch feature past it to tell you when you've overshot.

skills.title: Get lost on purpose
skills.detail: Once a month, deliberately drop your compass in your pocket and re-orient from terrain alone. That re-orientation is what selection is actually testing.

homework: Buy the compass this week. Cammenga 3H tritium, protractor, and a 1:50,000 map of local terrain. Not next month. This week.
source: TC 3-25.26 (Map Reading and Land Navigation) + Ruck Up or Shut Up ch. on Land Navigation (Walton)

title: Son Tay: The Raid That Rewrote Special Operations
summary: November 21, 1970 — 56 Green Berets hit a POW camp 23 miles from Hanoi and freed zero prisoners. Why the raid is still the DNA of every modern SOF hostage rescue.
takeaways: Ivory Coast / Kingpin, launched night of 20-21 Nov 1970 — 27 minutes on the ground, zero U.S. KIA
Planning cell run by BG Donald Blackburn; ground force by Col Bull Simons; assault led by Capt Dick Meadows
170+ full-scale rehearsals against the 'Barbara' mockup at Eglin AFB — home of 7th SFG today
Simons' element accidentally hit a nearby barracks (likely foreign advisors) — killed 100-200, then extracted to the real objective
Prisoners had been moved in July 1970 due to flooding; intel missed it
Consequence: NVA consolidated all POWs into Hanoi, ending most solitary/torture — the 'failed' raid materially improved POW conditions
Direct ancestor of Delta, JSOC (1980), and every DA hostage-rescue op through Abbottabad 2011
Volunteers were told nothing about the mission and stepped up anyway — the Simons filter

skills.title: Rehearse to unconscious
skills.detail: Whatever you're training — ruck cadence, pace count, weapons drills — run the boring rep until it's automatic. Simons ran 170 iterations because muscle memory survives contact.

skills.title: Learn the names
skills.detail: Blackburn, Simons, Meadows, Doc Kirby. Read Benjamin Schemmer's 'The Raid' (1976) before you ship. If a team sergeant asks why Meadows matters, you should have an answer.

skills.title: Volunteer without conditions
skills.detail: 500 men volunteered without being told the mission. When SFAS cadre give ambiguous tasks, execute without renegotiating — that's the filter.

homework: Pull up the Son Tay Raid entry tonight. Note the date — 21 November 1970. Put Blackburn, Simons, and Meadows in your notebook.
source: Son Tay Raid (Operation Ivory Coast/Kingpin), 20-21 Nov 1970; Schemmer, 'The Raid' (1976)

title: The Special Forces Groups: Where You Actually End Up
summary: SF isn't monolithic. Same tab, same beret — but the Group you're assigned to decides your region, language, partner forces, and mission tempo. Here's how the seven Groups map to the world.
takeaways: 5 active + 2 National Guard Groups; each aligned to a geographic combatant command
1st SFG — Indo-Pacific (JBLM + Okinawa); Korean, Thai, Tagalog, Mandarin
3rd SFG — AFRICOM (Fort Liberty); French + Arabic; Sahel and Horn CT fight
5th SFG — CENTCOM (Fort Campbell); Arabic/Dari; Horse Soldiers heritage
7th SFG — SOUTHCOM (Eglin AFB); Spanish/Portuguese; deepest partner-force ties
10th SFG — EUCOM (Fort Carson + Stuttgart); oldest Group, activated 1952
19th (UT) & 20th (AL) — National Guard, same standard, same tab
You don't pick — but a high DLAB score buys you options

skills.title: Map the Groups
skills.detail: Pin a world map with the 7 Groups and their AORs. When someone asks 'why that Group,' you have a real answer, not a vibe.

skills.title: DLAB prep
skills.detail: Start basic linguistic pattern recognition now. High DLAB = harder languages = Group choice leverage at the end of the Q-Course.

skills.title: Read one book per Group
skills.detail: Horse Soldiers (5th), Lions of Kandahar (3rd), Kill Bin Laden context. Build cultural literacy so cadre convos land.

skills.title: Language sample
skills.detail: Pick two candidate languages tied to Groups you'd want (e.g., Arabic for 5th, Russian for 10th). 15 min/day on Duolingo or Pimsleur — signal, not fluency.

skills.title: Regional current events
skills.detail: Read one long-form piece per week on the AOR you'd want. War on the Rocks, CTC Sentinel, Small Wars Journal. Free.

skills.title: Talk to a Group vet
skills.detail: SOWT and the r/specialforces AMAs. Ask about the day-to-day of the Group you're eyeing — not the door-kicking, the FID rotations.

skills.title: Kill the favoritism
skills.detail: Rehearse the mental frame 'I go where they send me and I get to work.' Rigid preference gets punished in the assignment cycle.

skills.title: Log a Group-of-the-week note
skills.detail: One paragraph in your prep journal each week on a different Group — mission, history, current fight. Seven weeks = full coverage.

homework: Study the map. When cadre asks which Group and why, 'I like the mountains' is not an answer. Have a reason.

title: Selection Is a Mental Event with a Physical Component
summary: The physical standards at Mackall are gettable. What separates the guys who finish from the guys who don't isn't conditioning — it's how they handle uncertainty, deprivation, and ambiguity when nobody is watching or scoring.
takeaways: Physical standards (15:00 2-mi, 12-min mile ruck at 50 lb, 60/60 PT, 8–12 pull-ups) are the entry ticket — not the differentiator.
Motivation dies around day 4. You need something duller and more durable.
Cadre engineer uncertainty, deprivation, and ambiguity — your own head fills in 'you're failing' before they do.
Disconnect effort from feedback: full effort into a vacuum, every event.
Shrink the timeline — next meal, next halt, next 100m. Small horizons are always survivable.
Make quitting a two-step process. Never act on the VW thought; push the decision to the next event.
Ego death is a requirement. Guys who blow up came in with a self-image they had to protect.
The body gets you to selection. The head gets you through it.

skills.title: Solo unwitnessed ruck
skills.detail: Once this week, do a 45–60 min ruck alone with no music, no watch check-ins, no social media post. Effort into a vacuum.

skills.title: Shrink-the-horizon drill
skills.detail: On your next hard session, ban thinking past the next 5 minutes. When the mind drifts to 'how much left,' pull it back to the current rep or the current 100m.

skills.title: VW-tabling rehearsal
skills.detail: When 'I could stop right now' shows up mid-workout, practice the response: 'I can stop at the next mile marker.' Move it. Never act on it in the moment.

skills.title: Ambiguity reps
skills.detail: One session this week: don't check pace, distance, or time until finished. Just run/ruck by feel until a pre-set endpoint. Get comfortable not knowing.

skills.title: Bad-weather deposit
skills.detail: If it rains or drops cold this week, that's the session you do NOT skip. This is the account you withdraw from at Mackall.

skills.title: Ego-check ruck
skills.detail: On your next group anything (even a run with a friend), practice being the guy at the back without commentary or excuse. Sit in it.

skills.title: Journal one 'kept promise' per day
skills.detail: End of each day, write the one thing you did today that you didn't feel like doing. That list is your durability, on paper.

skills.title: Cold-start habit
skills.detail: Pick one recurring moment — first pull-up set, first step of the morning run — where you go from zero to full effort with no ramp. Selection doesn't warm you up.

homework: The body gets you to selection. The head gets you through it. Train them both, but never confuse which one is the bottleneck.

title: Rucking: How Not to Blow Out Your Feet and Back
summary: Rucking ends more prep careers than Mackall does. It's not running-with-weight — it's its own gait. Foot strike, pack fit, feet care, load ramp, terrain, volume, recovery.
takeaways: It's a gait, not a run. Fast deliberate walk — bouncing or jogging under load is wrong.
Standard: 12 min/mi @ 45–55 lb on rolling terrain, miles at a time. Get there by walking fast, not running slow.
Cadence 120–130/min. Short quick steps, midfoot-to-heel, roll through, push off. Long strides shred knees.
Pack HIGH and TIGHT. Hip belt on iliac crest FIRST, then shoulders, then load lifters. Sagging ruck = a week of lumbar pain per 10 mi.
Feet: liner sock under wool, broken-in boots that fit YOU. Toenails short + straight. Hot spot = STOP and tape NOW.
Start at 35 lb. +5 lb every 2–3 weeks. No ankle weights, no stacked vests — train the specific load geometry.
Trails > roads. Selection isn't pavement. Flat area? Stairs or parking-garage repeats.
Never add mileage AND weight the same week. Ramp ≤ 10%/wk. Deload every 4th–5th week. Bones remodel during rest.

skills.title: Pack fit dry-run
skills.detail: Load 20 lb. Cinch hip belt on iliac crest, shoulders, load lifters. Walk 10 min. Adjust. Reload. Muscle-memorize the sequence.

skills.title: Cadence walk
skills.detail: Metronome app @ 125 BPM. 20 min walk stepping every beat. The ruck stride without the load.

skills.title: Boot break-in
skills.detail: Wear boots + wool socks + liners on 3 easy walks this week. Identify hot spots BEFORE they're under load.

skills.title: Foot care ritual
skills.detail: Trim nails short + straight tonight. Buy leukotape + moleskin. Practice taping a heel before you need to.

skills.title: Terrain scouting
skills.detail: Find one trail loop within 20 min of home. Note the mileage. This is your future ruck route.

skills.title: Stairs repeats
skills.detail: Parking garage or stadium. 10 min up-and-down at cadence. Builds calves + quads for the eventual load.

skills.title: Post-walk recovery flow
skills.detail: Feet elevated 15 min. Roll calves + hip flexors. Protein + carbs within 60 min. Rehearse it now.

skills.title: Ruck-gate PT
skills.detail: Every Saturday 2-mile time trial toward sub-16:00. That's what unlocks the actual load work.

homework: This week — ONE ruck. 45 lb, 6 mi, trail if possible. Focus on foot strike + pack fit. Zero blisters.

title: The ODA: Why It's Twelve Men
summary: The A-team's 12-man structure isn't arbitrary. Understand the ODA and you understand what SF actually does — the whole pipeline is built to produce one of these 12 slots.
takeaways: SF's core mission is unconventional warfare — small footprint, indigenous force, force multiplier. NOT primarily direct action.
12 men: 2 officers (18A captain + 180A warrant/continuity) + 10 NCOs.
Two of every specialty so the team can split into two 6-man elements: 18B weapons, 18C engineer, 18D medic (hardest MOS, ~1yr training), 18E comms.
One 18F intel + one 18Z team sergeant. The captain COMMANDS. The 18Z RUNS the team.
Twelve = small enough to move quiet, large enough for redundancy in every skill, large enough to split, large enough to spread the interpersonal load.
Structure evolved from OSS Jedburgh 3-man teams in WWII, which proved too small.
Every SFAS/Q-Course event is filtering for a guy who FITS into that 12 — not a lone wolf.
Pick your MOS with intent. Don't chase 18D for prestige; don't dodge it for length. Pick what you want to do for 15 years.

skills.title: Read one 18-series MOS deep
skills.detail: Pick 18B/C/D/E/F this week. Read the training pipeline, day-in-the-life downrange, career progression.

skills.title: Watch an ODA doc
skills.detail: Find a legit interview or doc (Team House podcast, SOF interviews). Note how team dynamics come up more than kit.

skills.title: Draft your MOS ranking
skills.detail: List 18B/C/D/E in order of interest with a one-sentence reason. Revisit monthly — your answer should sharpen.

skills.title: Learn the ODA org chart
skills.detail: Sketch it from memory: 18A, 180A, 18Z, and 2x each of B/C/D/E + 1x F. Quiz yourself Friday.

skills.title: Study Jedburgh history
skills.detail: One evening read on OSS Jedburgh teams — the DNA of the ODA. Understand why 3 was too small.

skills.title: Practice "quiet professional" reps
skills.detail: One situation this week where you'd normally speak up to be seen — don't. Just do the work. Peer evals start now.

homework: This week, read up on ONE 18-series MOS in depth. Just one. Know what a day in that job looks like downrange.

title: SFAS: What Actually Gets People Cut
summary: 3 weeks at Camp Mackall. Cadre don't teach — they watch. Every event is a data point and you never see the scoreboard. Here's what actually cuts guys.
takeaways: 3 phases: (1) individual assessment — PT, swim, obstacle, runs, ruck, land nav. (2) team week — ad-hoc teams, log/Zodiac/water can problems, never enough time. (3) Star Course / Long Walk — solo multi-day land nav with a ruck.
#1 reason guys don't select: VOLUNTARY WITHDRAWAL. More quit than get medical or peered. Most are physically capable. Ambiguity in the dark hours is the weapon.
#2: LAND NAV. Star Course especially. Can't shoot azimuth, pace-count broken terrain at night, re-attack a missed point → go home. Most trainable skill people show up under-prepared for.
#3: PEER EVALS. Teammates rank each other; cadre read it. Don't carry your share of the log = peered out. You can pass every physical event and still not select.
#4: INJURIES. Some bad luck; most are accumulated damage from ramping too fast in the 6 months before shipping.
Selection isn't won at Mackall. It's won in the 18-24 months before, in boring reps nobody sees.
Take VW off the table BEFORE you get on the bus. You can be injured out. You can be peered out. You cannot quit.

skills.title: Buy land nav kit
skills.detail: Lensatic compass, protractor, 1:50k topo maps of a local park. This is the highest-ROI purchase before ship.

skills.title: Pace count calibration
skills.detail: Measure 100m on flat ground, count your paces. Now do it uphill, downhill, in tall grass. Log each.

skills.title: Azimuth practice
skills.detail: Pick a distant landmark. Shoot the bearing with compass. Walk to it in a straight line. Repeat 5x.

skills.title: Night nav rep
skills.detail: One evening this week — walk a known 1-mile loop with headlamp OFF except at checkpoints. Get comfortable with the dark.

skills.title: Log carry drill
skills.detail: Solo prep: farmer-carry a heavy sandbag/log 100m, rest 30s, repeat 10x. Fatigue teaches you what "carrying your share" feels like.

skills.title: VW pre-commitment
skills.detail: Write on an index card: "I will not voluntarily withdraw." Keep it in your wallet. Read it on hard days.

skills.title: Injury-prevention audit
skills.detail: This week — one deload run (30 min easy), foam roll 2x, sleep 8hr min 5 nights. Habits > heroics.

homework: This week — one ruck with a REAL map and compass, no phone GPS. Find three points on foot. If that sounds easy, do it at night.
